sourceFacts.fact: A childhood upper respiratory infection can impair Eustachian tube ventilation and drainage, allowing middle-ear fluid to accumulate.
Fluid can persist after acute otitis media; effusion alone does not prove ongoing acute infection.

edges: can persist after acute symptoms settle
layoutSpecification: Title 'After a respiratory infection'. Use a three-stage left-to-right visual mechanism built from abstract objects, explicitly no ears, head, throat or bodily tube. Left: a small folded tissue and a round spiked respiratory-virus SYMBOL, labelled 'Respiratory infection'. Middle: two small abstract flow ribbons, one air swirl and one water drop, each narrowed by a simple gate icon; labels 'Less ventilation' and 'Less drainage'. Both ribbons feed the RIGHT stage, a shallow open glass bowl with pooled blue drops labelled 'Fluid can remain'. Beneath the bowl a small calendar with fading ochre symptom marks is labelled 'Acute symptoms may settle first'. Direction arrows all left-to-right. Draw no microbes within fluid and do not equate every effusion with active infection. All objects are visual metaphors, not a substitute anatomical pathway. NO snowflakes, wind, temperature symbols or cold-weather cues. Infection is the initiating concept; the virus icon is generic, not microbiological anatomy.
forbiddenAnatomy: No internal organ, eye, ear, brain, tissue or bone anatomy
No diagnostic image, patient-specific lesion appearance or literal anatomical pathway
